query: Taking nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 as the starting material, what single intervention could prevent its radiation-induced precipitation while retaining its negligible irradiation hardening and improving its suitability for practical bulk fabrication? Formulate one testable hypothesis for energetic-particle irradiation relevant to fusion service, including comparison with the unmodified alloy at approximately 8 dpa; identify the intervention and mechanism, predict quantitative or directional changes in precipitation, irradiation defects, and hardening, define the applicable irradiation and thermal boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and propose a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of hafnium (Hf) into the nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy will suppress the radiation‐induced segregation and subsequent Cr–V precipitation by modifying the local chemical short‐range order, while maintaining negligible irradiation hardening and simultaneously enhancing processing (bulk consolidation) characteristics.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 refractory high-entropy alloy showing a single-phase BCC structure with a bimodal grain size distribution and, upon irradiation, the formation of ~3–5 nm Cr–V-rich precipitates alongside negligible irradiation hardening.
generation.intervention: Addition of a minor fraction (approximately 7–8 atomic percent) of Hf to the base alloy to form a quinary system.
generation.conditions: Irradiation with energetic particles (e.g., 3-MeV ions) to approximately 8 dpa at elevated temperatures around 1073 K, representative of fusion reactor relevant service conditions; additional evaluation during powder consolidation/sintering relevant for bulk fabrication.
generation.structural_mediator: Modified short-range order and altered grain-boundary chemistry—Hf is expected to promote a more homogenized elemental distribution and reduce the driving force for Cr–V phase separation.
generation.mechanism: Hf addition is proposed to change the local thermodynamic landscape and atomic diffusion characteristics. By altering the short-range ordering tendencies, Hf reduces the preferential segregation of Cr and V that normally results in precipitate formation under irradiation. Simultaneously, the modified grain boundary composition can enhance sinterability and bulk consolidation due to improved diffusion kinetics during processing.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy, the Hf-doped quinary alloy will exhibit a significant reduction (or near elimination) in the size and area density of irradiation-induced Cr–V precipitates, maintain negligible irradiation hardening, and demonstrate improved bulk processing characteristics such as higher sintered density at equivalent consolidation temperatures.
generation.baseline: The unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy shows uniform irradiation-induced Cr–V precipitation (with precipitate sizes of ~3–5 nm) and only a slight increase in hardness after irradiation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to irradiation conditions up to ~8 dpa at around 1073 K as well as to processing methods (e.g., spark plasma sintering) used for bulk fabrication. It is assumed that the benefits of Hf addition manifest at these temperatures and irradiation doses.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extrapolates the stabilizing effects of Hf reported in quinary W–Ta–Cr–V–Hf systems (e.g., evidence from PMC10154406: high thermal stability section) to the specific case of W38Ta36Cr15V11 and its bulk processing. The influence of Hf on both microstructural evolution under irradiation and sintering behavior is not directly measured in the base alloy, so concentration optimization and comprehensive testing are needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: the baseline W38Ta36Cr15V11 and an Hf-doped variant (with ~7–8 at.% Hf replacing part of one of the constituents to maintain similar electron concentration and BCC structure). Subject both variants to energetic particle irradiation up to ~8 dpa at approximately 1073 K. Follow irradiation with detailed microstructural characterization (using atom probe tomography and TEM) and nanoindentation measurements. Additionally, fabricate bulk samples via spark plasma sintering to assess sinterability and densification.
measurements: APT to quantify elemental homogeneity and detect Cr–V precipitate volume fraction and size distribution.
TEM to visualize precipitate formation and defect structures.
Nanoindentation to measure hardness changes post-irradiation.
Density measurements and microstructural analysis of consolidated samples to assess bulk fabrication quality.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-doped alloy shows no significant reduction in the Cr–V precipitate density/size compared to the baseline, exhibits similar or increased irradiation-induced hardening, or does not demonstrate improved sinterability (e.g., if bulk samples fail to densify adequately), then the hypothesis is falsified.

These compositions are then manufactured experimentally to test both their ion irradiation and hardness responses, aiming at validating modeling predictions. The present work shows the development of a new class of a refractory HEA based on four elements: 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V in atomic percentages measured by both EDS and APT. Samples were grown using a magnetron sputtering deposition system from pure metal targets and characterized before and after irradiation. Microstructures present a single-phase BCC crystalline structure. The films show a bimodal grain size distribution with ~70% of the grains with sizes in the nanocrystalline regime (≤100 nm) and some regions of ultrafine grain sizes (100 to 500 nm). Concurrent TEM and APT analyses demonstrate the existence of a second phase rich in Cr and V, first forming lamella-like regions to transform to quasi-spherical precipitates after irradiation. Irradiations were carried out both in situ and ex situ at room temperature and 1073 K up to 8 dpa. A thorough analysis of the microstructure shows no sign of radiation-induced dislocation loops, confirming that the observed black spots are indeed second-phase particles.
